title: Processes vs threads
description: Learn the differences between processes and threads, and when to use each.

data.text: Modern computers can run many programs at the same time. The operating system makes this possible using two basic building blocks: processes and threads. Understanding the difference is essential for writing efficient, stable software.

A process is an independent program in execution. Each process has its own private memory space, its own environment variables, and its own file handles. If one process crashes, it cannot directly corrupt another process. The operating system isolates processes from each other for stability and security.

A thread is the smallest unit of execution inside a process. A single process can contain multiple threads, and those threads share the same memory space. This makes threads lightweight and fast to create, but it also means a bug in one thread can corrupt data used by another thread.

data.title: Processes vs threads at a glance

cards.title: Process
cards.description: An isolated program instance with its own memory space. Safe but heavier.

cards.title: Thread
cards.description: A lightweight execution path inside a process. Fast but shares memory with other threads.

data.title: Use processes when
items: You need strong isolation between tasks
Security boundaries matter, such as running untrusted code
A crash in one task must not affect others
You are working across different programming languages

data.title: Use threads when
items: Tasks need to share data frequently
You need low-latency communication between workers
The workload can be divided into smaller parallel chunks
You are building a responsive UI that must stay interactive

data.title: Thread safety matters
data.text: Because threads share memory, two threads modifying the same data at the same time can corrupt it. Use locks, atomic operations, or message passing to coordinate access.

items.question: Can one process contain another process?
items.answer: No. Processes are always peers managed by the operating system. A process can create child processes, but they remain separate execution contexts.

items.question: Do threads always run on different CPU cores?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Threads can also time-slice on a single core. Whether they run in parallel depends on the OS scheduler and available cores.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Processes are isolated and secure but heavier
Threads are lightweight and fast to create but share memory
Use processes for isolation and threads for shared-data efficiency
Thread safety is the main challenge when using multiple threads
data.takeaway: Choose processes when isolation is critical, and threads when speed and shared data are more important.
